concepts.title: The Relationship Between Vision and Language
concepts.one_liner: Vision and language are both mental models used to represent the world for higher-level cognition and decision making.
concepts.content: While vision and language might initially seem unrelated if language is viewed only as communication, another perspective suggests that language is a representation of the world used by the brain for higher-level cognition. Visual perception is similarly about representing the world and forming mental models that serve as a substrate for reasoning and decision making. From this perspective, both language and vision are solving essentially the same problem. This view is powerful, as language and vision can support each other in numerous ways within artificial intelligence systems.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding the deep connection between vision and language allows for the development of multimodal models that leverage the strengths of both to better represent the world.
concepts.recap_md:
- Language and vision are both internal representations of the world for reasoning.
- Both fields aim to form mental models that support decision making.
- Integrating the two allows vision systems to improve through language and vice versa.

key_passage.text: Visual perception is also about representing the world around us and forming mental models that act as a substrate for reasoning and decision making. From this perspective, both language and vision are trying to solve more or less the same problem.

motivation.text: The last few decades have seen enormous improvements in both computer vision and natural language processing. Naturally, there has been great interest in putting these two branches of artificial intelligence (AI) together.

concepts.title: Vision-Language Models (VLMs)
concepts.one_liner: Vision-language models (VLMs) are AI models that integrate visual and linguistic information.
concepts.content: In order to understand vision-language models (VLMs), we first need to understand a bit about language models.
concepts.motivation_md: VLMs are designed to bridge the gap between visual perception and linguistic description, enabling tasks like image captioning and visual question answering.
concepts.recap_md:
- VLMs combine computer vision and natural language processing.
- Understanding VLMs requires a foundational knowledge of how language models function.

concepts.one_liner: Natural language processing (NLP) is the field of AI focused on the interaction between computers and human language.

concepts.title: Word-Level Encoding
concepts.one_liner: Word-level encoding maps each unique word in a vocabulary to a unique one-hot code.
concepts.content: One option for representing text as numbers is to use a word-level encoding scheme, mapping each word in our vocabulary to a unique one-hot code. This requires $K$-dimensional one-hot codes for a vocabulary of $K$ different words.
concepts.motivation_md: To process text with neural networks, words must be converted into a numerical format that the model can interpret.
concepts.recap_md:
- Each word is represented by a unique one-hot vector.
- The vector dimension is equal to the size of the vocabulary ($K$).

concepts.title: Character-Level Encoding
concepts.one_liner: Character-level encoding assigns a one-hot code to each individual character rather than to whole words.
concepts.content: Instead of words, we could use a strategy where we assign a one-hot code to each character in our vocabulary. If we represent all alphanumeric characters and common punctuation marks, this might only require a few dozen codes. The disadvantage is that representing a single word now requires a sequence of one-hots rather than a single code, which the model must then account for.
concepts.motivation_md: Character-level encoding significantly reduces the vocabulary size and avoids the problem of out-of-vocabulary words, though it increases sequence length.
concepts.recap_md:
- Uses a small vocabulary of characters and punctuation.
- Words are treated as sequences of character codes.
- Reduces dimensionality but increases the complexity of modeling sequences.

concepts.title: Byte-Pair Encoding (BPE)
concepts.one_liner: Byte-pair encoding (BPE) is a subword encoding strategy that assigns codes to common substrings found in text.
concepts.content: A happy middle ground can be achieved using byte-pair encodings (BPE). In this approach, we assign a one-hot code to each small chunk of text. The chunks are common substrings found in text, like "th" or "ing." This strategy is popular in language models like the generative pretrained transformer (GPT) series and the contrastive language-image pretraining (CLIP) model.
concepts.motivation_md: BPE balances the efficiency of word-level encoding with the flexibility of character-level encoding, effectively handling rare words by breaking them into common sub-components.
concepts.recap_md:
- Encodes text using common substrings (subwords) rather than full words or single characters.
- Used in major models like GPT and CLIP.
- Provides a balance between vocabulary size and sequence length.

concepts.title: Text Tokenization
concepts.one_liner: Text tokenization converts one-hot encoded text sequences into dense token vectors via a projection matrix from the vocabulary dimensionality to a target dimensionality.
concepts.content: Once we have converted text into a sequence of one-hot codes, the next step is to convert these into tokens via a projection, $\mathbf{W}_{\texttt{tokenize}}$, from the one-hot dimensionality ($K$) to a target dimensionality for token code vectors ($d$). (see figure: Tokenizing text. Note that these steps can be implemented with a lookup table that simply stores the token code vector for each unique item in our vocabulary.) These steps convert an input string to tokens. For simplicity, word-level one-hot encoding is often shown rather than byte-pair encoding.
concepts.motivation_md: Raw text cannot be processed directly by neural networks. Tokenization maps discrete vocabulary items into a continuous vector space, allowing transformers and other architectures to perform mathematical operations on linguistic data.

concepts.title: Autoregressive Language Models

position.section_title: Learning Visual Representations from Language Supervision

concepts.one_liner: Autoregressive language models generate text by predicting each next vocabulary item based on the sequence of tokens generated so far.
concepts.content: To handle the output side, where we produce text as an output, we need to convert tokens back to text. The most common way to do this is to use an autoregressive model that predicts each next item in our vocabulary (word/character/byte-pair) given the sequence generated so far. Each prediction step can be modeled as a softmax over all $K$ possible items in our vocabulary.
concepts.motivation_md: While encoders map text to tokens, generative tasks require a mechanism to produce coherent sequences. Autoregressive modeling breaks down the complex task of sequence generation into a series of conditional probability predictions.
concepts.recap_md: - Predicts the next vocabulary item based on the preceding sequence.

concepts.title: Visual Representation Learning from Language Supervision

position.section_title: Learning Visual Representations from Language Supervision

concepts.one_liner: Language supervision uses free-form natural language as a pretext task to learn rich visual representations of scenes.
concepts.content: One approach of learning visual representations is to set up a pretext task that requires arriving at a good representation of the scene, using language association as the pretext task. Historically, image classification (associating an image with one of $K$ nouns) was a form of language supervision. However, human languages contain much richer linguistic structures than simple noun sets, including adjectives, verbs, and relational words. The most effective approach at scale is to train a vision system that associates images with free-form natural language, utilizing all the structure present in language.
concepts.motivation_md: Traditional supervised learning is limited by fixed label sets. Using natural language as supervision allows models to learn from the vast, diverse descriptions available on the internet, capturing more nuanced visual concepts than simple categories.
concepts.recap_md: - Uses language association as a pretext task for visual representation learning.

key_passage.text: train a vision system that associates images with free-form natural language

question.text: could we use richer linguistic structure to supervise vision?

motivation.text: Researchers have tried using all kinds of language structures to supervise vision systems, including adjectives and verbs, words indicating relationships between objects, and question-answer pairs. What seems to work best, once you reach a certain scale of data and compute, is to just use all the structure in language, and the simplest way to do this is to train a vision system that associates images with free-form natural language.

concepts.title: Contrastive Language-Image Pretraining (CLIP)

position.section_title: Learning Visual Representations from Language Supervision

concepts.one_liner: CLIP is a contrastive learning method that aligns co-occurring visual and linguistic views by maximizing the similarity between image and caption embeddings.
concepts.content:
Contrastive Language-Image Pretraining (CLIP) is a contrastive method in which one data view is the image and the other is a caption describing the image. Specifically, CLIP is a form of contrastive learning from co-occurring visual and linguistic views formulated as follows:

[FIGURE:7d5ab02809b91736]

where $\boldsymbol\ell$ represents an image, $\mathbf{t}$ represents text, $\mathbb{S}^{d_z}$ represents the space of unit vectors of dimensionality $d_z$, $f_{\ell}$ is the image encoder, and $f_t$ is the text encoder. Image inputs are represented as $[3 \times N \times M]$ pixel arrays, while text inputs are represented as $d_t$ dimensional tokens. The objective is a symmetric version of the InfoNCE loss. Both $f_\ell$ and $f_t$ output unit vectors via $L_2$-normalization, ensuring the denominator cannot dominate by pushing negative pairs infinitely far apart.
concepts.motivation_md: CLIP was designed to create a robust visual representation that understands natural language descriptions, enabling models to generalize to new visual tasks without needing task-specific labeled data.
concepts.recap_md: - Uses a symmetric InfoNCE loss to align image and text encoders.

concepts.title: CLIP Training Procedure

position.section_title: Learning Visual Representations from Language Supervision

concepts.one_liner: CLIP training involves maximizing the dot product between matched image-text pairs while minimizing it for all other pairings in a batch.
concepts.content:
To train CLIP, we first sample a batch of $N$ language-image pairs, $\{\mathbf{t}^{(i)}, \boldsymbol\ell^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^N$. Next, we measure the dot product between all these text strings and images using a language encoder $f_t$ and an image encoder $f_\ell$, producing text embeddings $\{\mathbf{z}^{(i)}_t\}_{i=1}^N$ and image embeddings $\{\mathbf{z}^{(i)}_\ell\}_{i=1}^N$. To compute the loss, we take the dot product $\mathbf{z}^{(i)}_\ell\cdot \mathbf{z}^{(j)}_t$ for all $i, j \in \{1,\ldots,N\}$. Terms where $i = j$ are positive pairs, and we seek to maximize these dot products. Terms where $i \neq j$ are negative pairs, and we seek to minimize these dot products.

(see figure: CLIP training for one batch of six language-image training examples. Green boxes are positive pairings (we seek to increase their value); these are the six training pairs. Red boxes are negative...)
concepts.motivation_md: By training on large batches of image-text pairs, the model learns to identify the specific features that link a description to its corresponding image, creating a shared semantic space.
concepts.recap_md: - Maximizes dot products for positive (matched) pairs and minimizes them for negative pairs.

key_passage.text: Next we embed measure the dot product between all these text strings and images using a language encoder $f_t$ and an image encoder $f_\ell$, respectively. To compute the loss, we take the dot product $\mathbf{z}^{(i)}_\ell\cdot \mathbf{z}^{(j)}_t$ for all $i, j \in \{1,\ldots,6\}$. Terms for which $i \neq j$ are the negative pairs and we seek to minimize these dot products (denominator of the loss); terms for which $i == j$ are the positive pairs and we seek to maximize these dot product (they appear in both the numerator and denominator of the loss).

concepts.title: CLIP Embedding Space and Visualization

position.section_title: Learning Visual Representations from Language Supervision

concepts.one_liner: The CLIP embedding space maps images and text to a shared hypersphere where small angles indicate high semantic similarity.
concepts.content:
After training, the text encoder $f_t$ and image encoder $f_\ell$ map to the same embedding space. In this space, the angle between a text embedding and an image embedding will be small if the text matches the image. The dot product between unit vectors is proportional to the angle between the vectors.

(see figure: CLIP @radford2021learning mapping diagram, using the same technique as described in @sec-neural_nets_as_distribution_transformers. To reduce dimensionality we apply t-SNE @tsne separately for the...)

In the image encoder, early layers may group images by color while later layers group by shape; in the text encoder, color and shape words are equally accessible. The final stage normalizes outputs so embeddings lie on the surface of a hypersphere. Text descriptions are embedded near matching image embeddings, though visualization in 2D (using kernel PCA or t-SNE) may have limitations.

(see figure: CLIP @radford2021learning joint embedding)
concepts.motivation_md: A shared embedding space allows the model to compare different modalities (vision and language) using simple geometric operations like dot products or cosine similarity.
concepts.recap_md: - Embeddings are $L_2$-normalized to lie on a hypersphere.

concepts.title: Zero-Shot Image Classification with CLIP

position.section_title: Learning Visual Representations from Language Supervision

concepts.one_liner: CLIP enables zero-shot image classification by comparing a query image embedding to embeddings of arbitrary text descriptions of classes.
concepts.content:
CLIP connects images to language, allowing the construction of novel image classifiers on the fly using natural language descriptions. To classify an image among a set of classes $a, b, \ldots$:

1. Embed each class description sentence into a vector: $\mathbf{z}_t^{a} = f_t(\mathbf{t}^{a}), \mathbf{z}_t^{b} = f_t(\mathbf{t}^{b}), \ldots$
2. Embed the query image into a vector: $\mathbf{z}_{\ell}^{q} = f_{\ell}(\boldsymbol\ell^{q})$.
3. Predict the class whose sentence embedding is closest (in angular distance) to the image embedding.

(see figure: Making a ``striped red circles'' (class $a$) versus ``polka dotted green square'' (class $b$) classifier using a trained CLIP. The CLIP model parameters are frozen and not updated. Instead the...)

This approach leverages the compositional power of language to distinguish complex concepts like "striped red circles" without further training.

[FIGURE:bbc557ba56150a05]
concepts.motivation_md: Traditional classifiers require retraining to learn new categories. Zero-shot classification allows a model to recognize concepts it has never seen as explicit labels by leveraging its general understanding of language.
concepts.recap_md: - Classifies images by finding the closest text embedding among candidate class descriptions.

key_passage.text: Given a set of sentences that describe images of classes a, b, and so on, Embed each sentence into a z-vector, Embed your query image into a z-vector, See which sentence embedding is closest to your image embedding; that's the predicted class.

motivation.text: CLIP connects the domain of images to the domain of language. This means that many of the powerful abilities of language become applicable to imagery as well. One ability that the CLIP paper showcased is making a novel image classifier on the fly.

concepts.title: Translating between Images and Text
concepts.one_liner: Modality translation involves using deep networks to forge links between disparate data types, such as images and text or sounds and lyrics.
concepts.content: It is possible to translate between entirely different data modalities (X2Y and Y2X). For any type of data X and any other type Y—such as images and sounds, music and lyrics, or amino acid sequences and protein geometry—deep networks can be used to forge links between these disparate domains of knowledge. These systems allow tools and discoveries from one domain to become applicable to other linked domains.
concepts.motivation_md: Translating between modalities allows models to transfer knowledge across different forms of data, enabling applications like text-to-image generation or automated music transcription.
concepts.recap_md: - Forges links between disparate domains of knowledge (e.g., images and sounds).

key_passage.text: For any type of data X, and any other type Y, there is, increasingly, a method X2Y (and Y2X) that translates between these two data types.

concepts.title: Modular Encoder-Decoder Translation
concepts.one_liner: One approach to solving translation problems is to hook up an encoder for the source domain to a decoder for the target domain.
concepts.content: One approach to solving X-to-Y translation problems is to do it in a modular fashion by hooking up an *encoder* for domain X to a decoder for domain Y. This approach is popular because powerful encoder and decoder architectures, and pretrained models, exist for many domains. If we have an encoder $f: \mathcal{X} \rightarrow \mathcal{Z}$ and a decoder $g: \mathcal{Z} \rightarrow \mathcal{Y}$, then we can create a translator simply by function composition, $g \circ f$.
concepts.motivation_md: This modular approach allows researchers to leverage existing, high-performance pretrained models for specific domains (like vision or language) and combine them to solve complex cross-domain translation tasks without building a monolithic system from scratch.
concepts.recap_md: - Translation can be achieved by composing an encoder $f$ and a decoder $g$ into a single function $g \circ f$.

concepts.title: Encoder-Decoder Alignment Strategies
concepts.one_liner: Encoder-decoder alignment can be achieved by finetuning the full composition or by training a latent-space mapping between frozen components.
concepts.content: To *align* the encoder and decoder we can follow several strategies. One is to simply finetune $g \circ f$ on paired examples of the target translation problem, $\{\mathbf{t}^{(i)}, \boldsymbol\ell^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^N$. Another option is to freeze $f$ and $g$ and instead train a translation function in latent space, $h: \mathcal{Z} \rightarrow \mathcal{Z}$, so that $g \circ h \circ f$ correctly maps each training point $\mathbf{t}^{(i)}$ to the target output $\boldsymbol\ell^{(i)}$.
concepts.motivation_md: Simply connecting a pretrained encoder and decoder is often insufficient because their latent spaces may not be naturally aligned; these strategies provide ways to bridge that gap using available paired data.
concepts.recap_md: - Alignment can be done by finetuning the entire end-to-end composition on paired data.

key_passage.text: One is to simply finetune g ∘ f on paired examples of the target translation problem, {t^(i), ℓ^(i)}_{i=1}^N. Another option is to freeze f and g and instead train a translation function in latent space, h: Z → Z, so that g ∘ h ∘ f correctly maps each training point t^(i) to the target output ℓ^(i).

concepts.title: Text-to-Image
concepts.one_liner: Text-to-image is the problem of synthesizing an image from a text description using generative models.
concepts.content: One amazing ability of modern generative models is to synthesize an image just from a text description, a problem called **text-to-image**. This can be achieved using any of the conditional generative models. We simply have to find an effective way to use text as the conditioning information to these models. (see figure: Text-to-image.) shows how this problem looks as a mapping from the space of text to the space of images. On the right is an example of such a system translating input text $\mathbf{t}$ to an output image $\hat{\boldsymbol\ell}$ that matches what the text describes. This new problem is not so different from representation learning and generative modeling diagrams seen previously.
concepts.motivation_md: Text-to-image synthesis allows humans to generate complex visual content using natural language, bridging the gap between symbolic communication and visual creation.
concepts.recap_md: - Text-to-image maps a text description $\mathbf{t}$ to a synthesized image $\hat{\boldsymbol\ell}$.

concepts.title: Text-to-Image with cVAE
concepts.one_liner: A conditional VAE for text-to-image uses a text encoder to provide the conditioning vector for an image decoder.
concepts.content: A conditional variational autoencoder (cVAE) can be used for text-to-image synthesis, as seen in the DALL-E 1 model. A cVAE for text-to-image can be trained just like a regular cVAE; the special thing is just that the encoder is a text encoder—a neural net that maps from text to a vector embedding. (see figure: Training a cVAE to perform text-to-image. The dotted lines indicate that the image encoder is only used during training; at test time, usage follows the solid path. In this cartoon we draw the output...) After training this model, we can sample from it by simply discarding the image encoder and instead inputting a random Gaussian vector to the decoder, in addition to providing the decoder with the text embedding. (see figure: Sampling from a trained cVAE.)
concepts.motivation_md: The cVAE framework provides a probabilistic way to map text to images, allowing for diverse outputs from the same text prompt by sampling from a latent distribution.
concepts.recap_md: - Training involves a text encoder and an image encoder to form the latent space.

concepts.title: Text-to-Image with Diffusion Models
concepts.one_liner: Conditional diffusion models generate images from text by inserting text embeddings into the layers of a denoising U-Net.
concepts.content: Text-to-image generation can be performed with a conditional diffusion model, an approach used by DALL-E 2 and other popular systems. A key challenge is effectively inserting text embeddings into the decoder. One way to do this is to insert text embedding vectors into each denoising U-Net, and even into multiple layers of each U-Net. This makes it very easy for the diffusion model to condition all of its decisions on the text information. (see figure: A text-to-image diffusion model.) A conditional diffusion model is very similar to a cVAE: at sampling time, both take text and Gaussian noise as input. However, while the VAE maps these to an image in a single forward pass, the diffusion model maps to an image via a chain of denoising steps.
concepts.motivation_md: Diffusion models often produce higher-quality and more detailed images than VAEs by iteratively refining noise into a coherent image guided by text conditioning.
concepts.recap_md: - Diffusion models condition on text by injecting embeddings into multiple layers of a denoising U-Net.

concepts.title: Image-to-Text (Image Captioning)
concepts.one_liner: Image-to-text, or image captioning, translates visual information into natural language descriptions using an image encoder and a text decoder.
concepts.content: Naturally, we can also translate in the opposite direction. We just need to use an *image encoder* (rather than a text encoder) and a *text decoder* (rather than a text encoder). In this direction, the problem can be called **image-to-text** or **image captioning**. This kind of translation is very useful because text is a ubiquitous and general-purpose interface between almost all domains of human knowledge. As an example of an image-to-text system, we will use a transformer to map the input image to a set of tokens, and we will then feed these tokens as input to an autoregressive text decoder, which is also implemented with a transformer. (see figure: Image-to-text using a small transformer with cross-attention. The edges in gray are cross-attention edges. Many variations of this architecture are possible. For example, each layer of the text...)
concepts.motivation_md: Translating images to text allows visual data to be processed by language models, enabling automated reasoning, accessibility through descriptions, and integration with vast textual knowledge bases.

concepts.title: Cross-Attention
concepts.one_liner: Cross-attention is a mechanism that allows text tokens to attend to image tokens, effectively integrating visual information into a text decoder.
concepts.motivation_md: Cross-attention provides a mathematically principled way for a model to 'look' at relevant parts of an image while generating each word of a text description.
concepts.recap_md: - Cross-attention allows text queries $\mathbf{Q}_t$ to interact with image keys $\mathbf{K}_\ell$ and values $\mathbf{V}_\ell$.

key_passage.text: This layer addresses the question of how to insert image tokens into a text model. The answer is quite simple: just let the text tokens attend to the image tokens.

motivation.text: The image tokens will emit their value vectors which will be mixed with the text token value vectors according to the attention weights to produce the next layer of tokens in the text decoder.

concepts.title: Text as a Visual Representation
concepts.one_liner: Text can be viewed as a high-level visual representation that captures the semantics of an image and interfaces directly with language models.
concepts.content: One way of thinking about image-to-text is as yet another visual encoder, where text is the visual representation. Just like we can represent an image in terms of its frequencies, its semantics and geometry, or its feature embeddings, we can also represent it in terms of a textual description of its content. (see figure: Four representations computed from the input on the left. The input image itself (its pixel values) is in fact a fifth representation of the scene.) Text is a powerful visual representation because it interfaces with language models. This means that after translating an image into text we can use language models to reason about the image contents.
concepts.motivation_md: Treating text as a representation allows us to apply the reasoning and logic capabilities of Large Language Models to visual data, which is otherwise difficult to 'reason' about in raw pixel form.
concepts.recap_md: - Text serves as a semantic visual representation alongside Fourier transforms or depth maps.

key_passage.text: One way of thinking about image-to-text is as yet another visual encoder, where text is the visual representation. Just like we can represent an image in terms of its frequencies (Fourier transform), its semantics and geometry (scene understanding), or its feature embeddings (DINO, CLIP, and others), we can also represent it in terms of a textual description of its content.

concepts.title: Visual Question Answering (VQA)
concepts.one_liner: Visual Question Answering (VQA) is a task where a system maps an image and a textual question to a textual answer.
concepts.content: Visual question answering (VQA) is a formulation of the goal to create fully general vision algorithms that can answer any question about an image, similar to a Turing test for visual intelligence. The problem statement in VQA is to make a system that maps an image and a textual question to a textual answer, as shown in @fig-vision_and_language-VQA_examples. (see figure: An example VQA system.) Creating a VQA system requires a text encoder for the question, an image encoder for the image, and a text decoder for the answer. These components can be hooked together using standard tools. The critical piece is to acquire training data of VQA examples, each taking the form of a tuple {[question, image], answer}.
concepts.motivation_md: VQA aims to develop general-purpose vision algorithms capable of answering arbitrary questions about visual data, serving as a benchmark for visual intelligence.
concepts.recap_md: - VQA systems map an image and a textual question to a corresponding textual answer.\n- The architecture typically combines a text encoder, an image encoder, and a text decoder.\n- Training requires datasets composed of question-image pairs and their ground-truth answers.

key_passage.text: Visual question answering (VQA) is one formulation of this goal. The problem statement in VQA is to make a system that maps an image and a textual question to a textual answer.

motivation.text: As AI systems become more general purpose, one goal is to make a vision algorithm that is fully general, so that you can ask it any question about an image. This is akin to a Turing test for visual intelligence.

concepts.title: Language as a Perceptual Representation
concepts.one_liner: Language can be viewed as a low-dimensional, abstracted perceptual representation that describes the world and interfaces with human knowledge.
concepts.content: From the perspective of vision, language is a perceptual representation. It is a way of describing "what is where" and much more in a low-dimensional and abstracted format that interfaces well with other domains of human knowledge. While there are many theories of how human language evolved, it may be the result of perceptual representation learning over the course of human evolution and cultural development. Language is one of the primary formats brains have arrived at as the best way to represent the "blooming, buzzing" sensory array around us.
concepts.motivation_md: This idea frames language not just as a communication tool, but as a structured way for the brain to represent and organize sensory information.
concepts.recap_md: - Language acts as an abstracted, low-dimensional format for representing perceptual data.\n- It may be the result of perceptual representation learning over human evolution.\n- This representation allows visual information to interface with broader domains of human knowledge.

prereq.rationale: CLIP is a concrete implementation of the idea of using free-form language as a supervision signal for vision.
The training procedure implements the specific encoders and objective defined in the CLIP framework.
The shared embedding space is the direct result of the contrastive training procedure.
Zero-shot classification with CLIP requires the image and text to be mapped to the same space where angular distance can be measured.
The text explicitly states that understanding VLMs requires a prior understanding of language models.
Tokenization is the subsequent step after text has been converted into a sequence of one-hot codes.
The concept conceptualizes the output of image-to-text systems as a specific type of visual representation.
The primary advantage of using text as a representation is its compatibility with language models for downstream reasoning.
Visual Question Answering is a core task and application within the broader framework of Vision-Language Models.
This concept provides a specific functional interpretation of the broader relationship between vision and language discussed earlier.
This technique is a modular implementation of the general concept of translating between modalities using function composition.
Alignment strategies like finetuning or latent mapping are necessary to ensure the composed encoder and decoder work together effectively.

overlay.rationale: VLMs are the primary architectural implementation of the conceptual relationship between vision and language.
Character-level encoding is presented as an alternative to word-level encoding with different trade-offs in vocabulary size and sequence length.
BPE is described as a 'happy middle ground' between word-level and character-level encoding.
VQA is closely related to image captioning (image-to-text), but adds a specific textual query that conditions the generated output.
While the previous section discussed text as a specific visual representation, this concept generalizes the idea to language as a fundamental perceptual format.
While both use text and noise, VAEs generate images in a single pass, whereas diffusion models use a chain of denoising steps.
Image-to-text is the inverse problem of text-to-image, translating visual data back into natural language descriptions.
